imageInfo.caption: Modern map of the Cuman-Kipchak lands in the thirteenth century, running from the Danube to the Irtysh, with Hungary, the Rus' principalities and the Volga Bulgars on their borders.
imageInfo.creator: Photo Balkan (Wikimedia Commons)
imageInfo.note: A modern reconstruction, not a period document, and the faint grey lines behind it are present-day state borders the file draws in for orientation. It shades Cumania as a single red state, which it never was: clans under their own khans, with no capital, no central authority and no written language, and the eastern limit towards the Irtysh is an estimate. The period it gives, 1200 to 1241, closes with the Mongol conquest that ended the confederation, and the neighbours named — the Kingdom of Hungary, the Principalities of Rus', the Sultanate of Anatolian Seljuq and the Eastern Roman Empire — are the powers the Cumans fought and served. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary: The Cumans were the Turkic confederation that ruled the steppe from the Danube to the Volga in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, fought and served every power around them, and were shattered by the Mongols in 1223.
overview: A people with no state, no capital and no writing, who nonetheless decided the fate of Byzantine, Rus' and Hungarian politics for two hundred years — and then supplied Egypt with its sultans.
knownFor: Ruled the Desht-i Qipchaq, the steppe from the Danube to the Volga.
Fought the Rus' principalities for a century and a half, and married into them.
Provided the forty thousand horsemen who destroyed the Pechenegs at Levounion in 1091.
Were broken by the Mongols at the Kalka in 1223 and fled west into Hungary.
Supplied, through the slave markets, the Kipchak Mamluks who ruled Egypt and Syria.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Cumans — Polovtsy to the Rus', Kipchaks in the Islamic sources — moved west across the steppe in the eleventh century and displaced the Pechenegs and the Oghuz from the grasslands north of the Black Sea.

They were never a state. What the sources call Cumania was a confederation of clans under their own khans, without a capital, a central authority or a written language, occupying the largest continuous grassland in Europe.

That did not make them marginal. For two centuries no war in the northern Balkans, the Rus' lands or the Hungarian plain was fought without Cuman cavalry on one side or both, and the Byzantine Empire owed them one of its most important victories.

contentSections.title: Names and Identity
paragraphs: This people carries more names in the sources than almost any other in the archive, and the multiplicity is itself evidence: each neighbour met a different part of a confederation that had no collective word for itself in general use.

The Islamic geographers write Qıpçaq, and the great steppe they held is the Desht-i Qipchaq, the Kipchak plain — the name with the best claim to being what they called themselves. The Rus' chronicles say Polovtsy, from a root meaning pale or fallow, which the German sources echo as Falben and the Latin as Pallidi. The Byzantines and the Latin west say Cumani, whence the English Cumans. Hungarian has Kun, and the district in the Hungarian plain where the refugees of 1239 were settled is still called Kunság.

Modern scholarship generally treats Cuman and Kipchak as two wings of one confederation rather than as synonyms, with the Cumans the western group and the Kipchaks the eastern, but the sources use the words loosely and often interchangeably, and no line drawn between them survives close examination. The Codex Cumanicus, a phrasebook compiled by Italian merchants and German missionaries around 1300, is the only substantial record of the language and was written to sell things to them and convert them — which is to say that even the linguistic evidence reaches us through outsiders with an errand.

contentSections.title: The steppe confederation
paragraphs: Their organisation was the standard steppe pattern: clans grouped into larger units under khans, cooperating for large campaigns and operating separately the rest of the time.
They lived by herding, by raiding settled neighbours, by charging for passage, and increasingly by selling captives — and, in the end, by being sold themselves.

The stone figures they set over their burial mounds are the largest body of physical evidence they left: thousands of them once stood across the steppe, and they are the closest thing to a Cuman self-portrait that exists.

contentSections.title: Major figures
paragraphs: As with the Pechenegs, the named khans are the ones outsiders recorded, and the list reflects who fought whom rather than who mattered.

Tugorkan and Bönek are the khans who led the Cuman force at Levounion in 1091 and then spent the following decade raiding the Rus' — Tugorkan was killed outside Pereyaslavl in 1096, having in the meantime married his daughter to the prince of Kiev.

Köten is the last and most consequential: the khan who led the survivors of the Mongol invasion into Hungary in 1239, was granted lands in exchange for conversion, and was murdered in Pest by a mob who believed the Cumans were Mongol spies — shortly before the Mongols arrived and destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohi.

contentSections.title: Religion and conversion
paragraphs: Cuman religion before the thirteenth century is known almost entirely from hostile description and from what was buried with the dead. The sources describe a Tengrist world of sky-worship, shamans and oath rituals — a peace sworn over a dog cut in half with a sabre appears in more than one Rus' account — and the kurgan steles, which hold a vessel at the waist with both hands, are usually read as ancestor figures fed by the living.

Latin Christendom came at them as a frontier to be worked. Dominican missionaries were active on the steppe from the 1220s, and in 1228 a bishopric of Cumania was founded in what is now Wallachia and Moldavia, with a Cuman chief baptised alongside his followers — an event the papacy treated as the opening of a new Christian province and the Hungarian crown as the basis of a claim to the territory.

Conversion in earnest came only with defeat. The price of asylum in Hungary in 1239 was baptism, and Köten accepted it; the Cumans settled on the plain were Christianised over generations, slowly enough that royal decrees were still legislating against pagan practice a century later. Those absorbed into the Golden Horde went the other way, into Islam, and the Kipchaks sold into Egypt became the Mamluk sultans of a Muslim state.

contentSections.title: Byzantium, the Rus' and Hungary
paragraphs: Their relationship with the Byzantine Empire was mercenary in the exact sense. In 1091 Alexios I hired forty thousand of them and destroyed the Pechenegs at Levounion; in other decades they raided the same frontier they had been paid to defend.

With the Rus' the relationship was continuous war and continuous intermarriage. Cuman raids are the background to a century and a half of Rus' history and to the Tale of Igor's Campaign, and several Rus' princes had Cuman mothers.

With Hungary it ended in settlement. The Cumans who fled the Mongols were given land in the Hungarian plain, and the region of Kunság still carries their name; their language survived there into the seventeenth century.

contentSections.title: The Mongols
paragraphs: In 1223 a Mongol reconnaissance force under Jebe and Subutai came round the Caucasus and attacked the Cumans, who appealed to the Rus' princes for help.
The combined Cuman and Rus' army was destroyed at the Kalka River. It is the first encounter between the Mongols and either people, and it went badly enough to be remembered as a portent.

The full invasion came in 1237. Cumania was destroyed as a political entity, and the survivors split: some submitted and were absorbed into the Golden Horde, some fled to Hungary and Bulgaria, and very large numbers were sold into slavery.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The largest consequence was one nobody intended. Kipchak captives sold through the Black Sea slave markets became the military slaves of the Ayyubid sultans of Egypt, and in 1250 those Mamluks took the state for themselves.

The Mamluk sultanate that resulted was Kipchak in origin and ruled Egypt and Syria for two and a half centuries — it stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, and it was a Kipchak-born sultan, Baibars, who destroyed Antioch in 1268.
So a steppe confederation with no writing and no capital ended up supplying the dynasty that halted the Mongols and destroyed the crusader principality of Antioch.

timeline.description: The khan who fought at Levounion dies outside Pereyaslavl, having married his daughter to the prince of Kiev.

timeline.title: The Tale of Igor's Campaign
timeline.description: A failed Rus' expedition against the Cumans becomes the most famous poem in early Slavic literature.

timeline.title: The bishopric of Cumania
timeline.description: A Latin see is founded on the steppe frontier and a Cuman chief is baptised with his followers.

timeline.description: A Mongol reconnaissance force destroys a combined Cuman and Rus' army.

timeline.title: Cumania destroyed
timeline.description: The Mongol invasion ends the confederation; survivors are absorbed, flee west, or are sold into slavery.

timeline.title: Köten enters Hungary
timeline.description: The khan leads survivors into the Hungarian plain and is murdered in Pest as a suspected Mongol spy.

timeline.title: The Mamluks take Egypt
timeline.description: Kipchak military slaves seize the Ayyubid state and found a sultanate that lasts two and a half centuries.

armsImageInfo.caption: The Cumans bore no coat of arms; they set stone figures like this twelfth- or thirteenth-century one, found at Stadnytsia in Ukraine, over their burial mounds.
armsImageInfo.creator: Unknown Cuman sculptor; photographed by Silar (Wikimedia Commons)
armsImageInfo.note: The Cumans left no writing, no coinage and no heraldry, so the kurgan steles stand in for an emblem: they are the confederation's own work and the largest body of evidence it left. This one comes from Stadnytsia, near Hleshchava in western Ukraine, and the photograph was taken where it now stands, in the Archaeological Museum in Kraków; the file gives no excavation record, no height and no findspot closer than the village. The figure wears a conical hat and holds a vessel at the waist with both hands, the standard gesture of these statues, and the image is a crop from the photographer's wider view. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: Cuman stone figures from Ukraine, carved between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries to stand over graves and now in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
sectionImages.creator: Cuman craftsmen; photographed in the Neues Museum
sectionImages.note: These are the Cumans' own work, which makes them rare: like the Pechenegs, the Cumans left no writing, and almost everything else known about them comes from the people they fought. The figures hold vessels at the waist and stood over burial mounds across the steppe. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: A modern replica of a thirteenth-century Kipchak masked helmet, photographed in 2013 in the Archaeological Museum in Kraków.
sectionImages.creator: Modern replica; photographed by Silar
sectionImages.date: photographed 2013; the original type of the thirteenth century
sectionImages.source: Archaeological Museum in Kraków, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: This is a reconstruction, not an excavated object, and the museum displays it as such. Masked helmets of this form are found across the western steppe and in the Rus' lands in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and are associated with Cuman and other nomad horsemen; the face mask, the tall crown and the mail attachment points are the features the surviving originals share. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: A page of the Codex Cumanicus, the Cuman glossary and phrasebook compiled about 1300, with a bird drawn in the margin.
sectionImages.creator: Italian merchants and German missionaries; unknown scribes
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca Marciana, Venice, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The only substantial record of the Cuman language, and it exists because outsiders had business with its speakers: the Italian half is a merchants' glossary of Latin, Persian and Cuman, and the German half carries missionary material, including the Lord's Prayer and the Creed in Cuman. The single manuscript survives in Venice, and the marginal drawings are the scribes' own. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: Cumans with their wagons in a miniature of the Radziwiłł Chronicle, a fifteenth-century Rus' copy of a thirteenth-century illustrated original.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown illuminator of the Radziwiłł Chronicle
sectionImages.source: Library of the Russian Academy of Sciences, St Petersburg, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The covered carts are the vezhi of the Rus' chronicles, the wagon-tents that carried a Cuman camp and its families and were drawn into a laager when the camp was attacked. Every khan named in this section — Tugorkan, Bönek, Köten — reaches us through a source of this kind, written by the people they raided or the people who hired them. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: Ladislaus IV of Hungary, son of a Cuman princess, shown in Cuman dress in the Illuminated Chronicle of about 1360.
sectionImages.creator: Workshop of the Illuminated Chronicle; unknown illuminator
sectionImages.source: National Széchényi Library, Budapest (Chronicon Pictum), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: In 1279, under a papal legate, Ladislaus swore that the Cumans settled on the Hungarian plain would leave their tents for houses and give up their idols and rites. The decrees were repeated because they were not obeyed, the king kept Cuman company and was excommunicated for it, and he was murdered by Cumans in 1290 — which is a fair measure of how far conversion had actually gone two generations after the settlement. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: Saint Ladislaus wrestling a Cuman warrior while the abducted girl cuts at him, painted about 1419 on the church wall at Dârjiu in Transylvania.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Transylvanian wall painter
sectionImages.source: Fortified church of Dârjiu (Székelyderzs), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The Saint Ladislaus legend was painted in dozens of Hungarian churches and is the standard medieval Hungarian image of a steppe enemy: tall hat, bow case, a duel on foot after the pursuit. It commemorates the raid defeated at Cserhalom in 1068, whose raiders were probably Pechenegs or Oghuz rather than Cumans, so the Cuman of the fresco is a type rather than a portrait. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The battle of the Kalka River in 1223, in a miniature of the Illustrated Chronicle of Ivan the Terrible, painted in the 1560s.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Muscovite illuminators
sectionImages.note: Painted more than three centuries after the battle by Muscovite artists who dressed everyone in the armour of their own day, and it is a Rus' account: the Cumans who asked the Rus' princes for help are not distinguished from them in the picture. Their khan Köten was the brother-in-law of Mstislav the Bold, which is why the appeal was heard at all. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: An enthroned Mamluk ruler with his attendants, inlaid in silver and gold on the brass basin known as the Baptistère de Saint Louis, made about 1320 to 1340.
sectionImages.creator: Muhammad ibn al-Zayn
sectionImages.source: Musée du Louvre, Paris (LP 16), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The basin is signed six times by its maker and was produced in Mamluk Egypt or Syria; it later entered the French royal collection and was used for royal baptisms, which is where its misleading name comes from. The sultanate whose court it shows was founded by Kipchak military slaves and ruled by them for generations, so this is what became of a large part of the Cuman population after 1241. The identification of the enthroned figure with any particular sultan is not settled. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
